body:
Why Alexander entered northwestern India

In the 4th century BCE, the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent was connected with the Persian Empire and the kingdoms of Central Asia. Alexander III of Macedon, commonly called Alexander the Great, defeated the Persian Empire and extended his conquests eastwards. After establishing control over important territories in Central Asia, he advanced towards the Indian subcontinent in 327 BCE.

Alexander's Indian campaign was mainly confined to the northwestern region, particularly areas around the Indus and its tributaries. It was not a conquest of the entire Indian subcontinent. Powerful kingdoms, including Magadha in the Gangetic plains, remained outside his control.

The advance through Taxila

Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush region and advanced towards the Indus. At Taxila, the local ruler, commonly known as Ambhi or Taxiles in Greek accounts, accepted Alexander's authority and assisted him. Ambhi's cooperation was connected with his rivalry with Porus, who ruled territory farther east, particularly between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers.

This illustrates an important feature of the campaign: Alexander did not face a single united Indian army. Different rulers responded according to their own political interests. Some resisted him, while others formed alliances.

The Battle of Hydaspes, 326 BCE

In 326 BCE, Alexander fought Porus at the Battle of Hydaspes. Hydaspes is the ancient Greek name for the Jhelum River, located in present-day Pakistan.

Porus commanded an Indian army that included war elephants. Alexander's Macedonian forces won the battle, but the resistance offered by Porus was substantial. After the victory, Alexander allowed Porus to continue ruling his territory under Macedonian supremacy and entrusted him with additional areas.

Hydaspes = Jhelum River. The battle was fought in 326 BCE between Alexander and Porus. Alexander won, but Porus was retained as a subordinate ruler.

Why the campaign stopped at the Beas

Alexander wished to continue farther east. However, his soldiers refused to advance beyond the Hyphasis River, the ancient Greek name for the Beas, in 326 BCE.

The army had already endured years of campaigning. Exhaustion, difficult climatic conditions and concern about further resistance contributed to its unwillingness to continue. Alexander therefore abandoned his eastward advance.

He returned towards the Indus, organised the movement of his forces downstream and withdrew from the region in 325 BCE. He died at Babylon in 323 BCE.

Consequences of Alexander's invasion

Alexander's direct political control over Indian territories was limited and short-lived. Following his death, Macedonian authority in the northwest weakened as his successors competed for power.

Nevertheless, the campaign strengthened political and geographical contacts between the northwestern subcontinent and the Hellenistic world. These contacts continued through subsequent Greek-speaking kingdoms, diplomacy and trade.

Chandragupta Maurya established the Mauryan Empire around 321 BCE. Later, Megasthenes served as a Greek ambassador at his court. This illustrates continued diplomatic interaction between the Greek-speaking world and Indian rulers after Alexander's campaign.

The Indo-Greek kingdoms of the 2nd century BCE were not established directly by Alexander during his invasion. They emerged considerably later through political developments in Bactria and northwestern India.

Prelims focus

  • Alexander advanced into northwestern India in 327 BCE.
  • The Battle of Hydaspes was fought in 326 BCE between Alexander and Porus.
  • Hydaspes is the Jhelum River; Hyphasis is the Beas River.
  • Ambhi of Taxila cooperated with Alexander.
  • Alexander's eastward advance stopped at the Beas after his army refused to proceed.
  • Trap: Alexander did not conquer Magadha or establish the later Indo-Greek kingdoms.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2: Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 32 and 50; Oxford University Press, Alexander the Great: The Anabasis and the Indica, Book 5 overview, consulted 19 November 2026; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Alexander the Great, section Invasion of India, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Alexander's Campaign in Northwestern India (327–325 BCE)

body:
Who were the Indo-Greeks?

The term Indo-Greeks refers to Greek-speaking rulers who established kingdoms in parts of northwestern India and adjoining regions, mainly during the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.

Following Alexander's conquests, Greek-speaking political settlements continued in the regions west and northwest of India. In the 3rd century BCE, an independent Greco-Bactrian kingdom emerged in Bactria, a region covering parts of present-day Afghanistan and Central Asia. Some Greco-Bactrian rulers later extended their power south of the Hindu Kush into northwestern India. These rulers are called Indo-Greeks.

The distinction is geographical as well as political: Greco-Bactrian generally refers to the Greek kingdom centred in Bactria, while Indo-Greek refers to Greek rulers and kingdoms established south of the Hindu Kush, including territories in the northwestern subcontinent.

Menander and the kingdom of Sagala

Menander I, also called Milinda in Buddhist literature, was one of the most prominent Indo-Greek rulers. He ruled in the 2nd century BCE and is traditionally associated with Sagala, identified with modern Sialkot in Pakistan.

The Buddhist work Milindapanha, meaning Questions of Milinda, presents a dialogue between King Milinda and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. The dialogue explains Buddhist ideas through questions and answers.

Menander's association with Buddhism is therefore an important part of the literary tradition. However, the dialogue should not be treated as a verbatim historical record of an actual conversation, and the precise circumstances of Menander's personal religious commitment are not securely established.

Menander = Milinda. Nagasena is the monk associated with him in the Milindapanha. Sagala = modern Sialkot.

Why Indo-Greek coins are important

Indo-Greek rulers introduced an important development in the coinage of the subcontinent: coins bearing the names and portraits of rulers. Earlier Indian punch-marked coins generally displayed symbols rather than a ruler's portrait and written name.

Many Indo-Greek coins carried bilingual inscriptions. One side commonly used Greek, while the other used an Indian language, usually Prakrit written in the Kharosthi script.

These coins served ordinary economic and political purposes. They also allowed rulers to communicate their identity to different linguistic communities living within their territories.

Political and cultural significance

Indo-Greek rule connected the northwestern subcontinent with the Hellenistic world. Greek-speaking rulers interacted with Indian communities, adopted local practices and issued coins intended for subjects who spoke different languages.

Their power gradually weakened as Central Asian groups, including the Shakas and Yuezhi, advanced into regions previously controlled by Greek-speaking kingdoms. Political authority did not change everywhere at the same time, and Indo-Greek and other ruling groups sometimes occupied neighbouring or overlapping territories.

Prelims focus

  • Indo-Greek kingdoms were prominent in northwestern India during the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.
  • They developed from the expansion of Greek-speaking rulers associated with Bactria.
  • Menander I is called Milinda in Buddhist literature.
  • Milindapanha associates Milinda with the monk Nagasena.
  • Indo-Greek coins commonly carried ruler portraits and bilingual Greek-Prakrit inscriptions.
  • Trap: Kharosthi is a script; Prakrit is a language.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2: Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 44–47 and 50; Osmund Bopearachchi, Indo-Greek Dynasty, Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. XIII, Fasc. 1, pp. 96–97, updated 2012, consulted 19 November 2026; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Logic in Classical Indian Philosophy, discussion of the Milindapanha, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Typical Indo-Greek coins pair a ruler’s portrait and Greek name with Prakrit in Kharosthi; earlier punch-marked coins generally show symbols.

title: Hellenistic Rule after Alexander: The Indo-Greeks

body:
Origin and arrival of the Shakas

The Shakas, also called Sakas or Indo-Scythians, were peoples of Central Asian origin. Their movement towards the northwest of the Indian subcontinent was connected with broader migrations and political pressures across Central Asia.

From about the 1st century BCE, Shaka rulers established authority in parts of northwestern and western India. Their political presence overlapped with the later stages of Indo-Greek rule and, subsequently, with Kushan power in some regions.

The Shakas should not be confused with the Indo-Greeks. Although both ruled in northwestern India, the Indo-Greeks belonged to the Greek-speaking political tradition associated with Bactria, while the Shakas were of Central Asian Scythian origin.

Where did the Shakas establish power?

Shaka groups entered through northwestern regions and established kingdoms in different parts of the subcontinent. Their influence became especially important in western India, including areas associated with Gujarat, Saurashtra, Kachchh and Malwa.

These territories connected inland towns with routes towards the western coast. Political control over important centres and routes could provide rulers with revenue from commercial activities.

Kshatrapas and Mahakshatrapas

The title Kshatrapa is related to the term satrap, meaning a provincial ruler or governor in the Iranian political tradition. Mahakshatrapa means great satrap and was used as a higher royal title.

In western India, Shaka ruling houses became known as the Western Kshatrapas. They exercised authority over important parts of Gujarat and adjoining regions during the early centuries CE.

Some notable rulers associated with Shaka power in western India include Nahapana, Chashtana and Rudradaman I. For the core prelims syllabus, the most important of these is Rudradaman because of his connection with a major inscription at Junagadh in Gujarat.

Shaka identifies the people or ruling groups of Central Asian origin. Kshatrapa and Mahakshatrapa are titles used by rulers. The terms do not refer to separate peoples.

The Shaka era

The Shaka era begins in 78 CE. This is an important chronological fact, but the beginning of the era must not be confused with the arrival of the Shakas in India, which occurred earlier.

Older textbook traditions sometimes associated 78 CE with Kanishka's accession. However, the precise chronology of Kanishka has been revised and remains distinct from the securely established starting year of the Shaka era.

Prelims focus

  • Shakas were also known as Sakas or Indo-Scythians.
  • They were of Central Asian origin, unlike the Greek-speaking Indo-Greeks.
  • Shaka rule became important in northwestern and western India.
  • The Western Kshatrapas were associated with Gujarat and neighbouring regions.
  • Kshatrapa means satrap; Mahakshatrapa means great satrap.
  • Trap: The Shaka era begins in 78 CE, but Shaka political activity in India began earlier.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2: Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 35 and 50; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Indo-Scythian Dynasty, consulted 19 November 2026; e-PG Pathshala, Indian Epigraphy, Module IC / I Epi / 29: Junagadh Inscription of Rudradaman, section 1, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Shaka influence moved from Central Asia into the northwestern subcontinent, then towards Gujarat, Saurashtra, Kachchh and Malwa in western India.
pictures.caption: Origin and regions associated with Shaka rule.

title: Shakas: Central Asian Migrants and Western Kshatrapas

body:
Rudradaman I and his Gujarat connection

Rudradaman I was an important ruler of the Western Kshatrapas, a Shaka ruling house in western India. He held the title Mahakshatrapa and ruled during the 2nd century CE.

His most important connection with Gujarat is the Junagadh rock inscription near Girnar. The inscription is dated to Shaka year 72, corresponding approximately to 150–151 CE.

It is written in the Sanskrit language using the Brahmi script. It is an important early example of an extended Sanskrit royal eulogy, or prashasti, in prose. A prashasti is a record praising a ruler and describing his achievements.

Rudradaman I: Junagadh, Girnar, Sanskrit, Brahmi, Shaka year 72, approximately 150 CE. These facts identify the ruler and inscription in objective questions.

The Sudarshana Lake

The inscription records the history and restoration of the Sudarshana Lake near Girnar. The lake had been created during the Mauryan period and was part of a water-management system.

According to the inscription, the main stages were:

  • Chandragupta Maurya's reign: Pushyagupta, a provincial governor, constructed the lake.
  • Ashoka's reign: Tushaspha, a governor described with the title Yavanaraja, added channels to the water system.
  • Rudradaman I's reign: A severe storm damaged the embankment. The lake was restored under Rudradaman's authority, with the work carried out by Suvisakha, the provincial governor of Anarta and Saurashtra.

Why the inscription matters

The inscription provides a direct historical connection between Mauryan administration and the later Western Kshatrapas in Gujarat. It also shows that a major public water structure could be maintained and repaired under different ruling dynasties.

The ruler identified with the lake's original construction is Chandragupta Maurya, through his governor Pushyagupta. The ruler associated with its important later restoration is Rudradaman I. These two contributions must not be interchanged.

The same inscription is also important because of its language. The correct association is Sanskrit language and Brahmi script, not Sanskrit written in Kharosthi.

Prelims focus

  • Rudradaman I was a Western Kshatrapa ruler of the 2nd century CE.
  • His Junagadh inscription is located near Girnar in Gujarat.
  • It is dated to Shaka year 72, approximately 150–151 CE.
  • The inscription is in Sanskrit, written in Brahmi script.
  • Pushyagupta built the Sudarshana Lake under Chandragupta Maurya; Suvisakha carried out its restoration under Rudradaman.
  • Trap: Rudradaman repaired the lake; he was not its original builder.

[e-PG Pathshala, Indian Epigraphy, Module IC / I Epi / 29: Junagadh Inscription of Rudradaman, sections 1–5, especially Location, Script and Language and Summary of the Content, consulted 19 November 2026; F. Kielhorn, Junagadh Rock Inscription of Rudradaman, Epigraphia Indica, Vol. 8, pp. 42–49, translation consulted through the Pramana digital edition on 19 November 2026.]
